Speaking to the dead

By: Sinethemba Nogude | Production

Proposal


Show:

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
We have a behind the scenes look at one of the busiest morgues in the Country

Unique Selling Point:
It's South Africa’s busiest morgue processing over 3000 bodies annually, on top of processing hundreds of unidentified corpses. We look at the men and women who you might ultimately meet after you take your final breath. We follow them on one of their busy shifts as they try to meet tight deadlines -in finding the cause of death and identifying unidentified bodies.


Summary:
This will be an exclusive behind the scenes look at one of the country's busiest morgues, processing an average of 3000 bodies a year. We will look at the dedicated workers who on a daily basis deal with death. We will also look at their world-renowned Identification Unit, which is tasked with trying to solve their ultimate forensic conundrum:identifying the many unclaimed bodies that come through their doors, we ill meet Dr. Candice Hansmeyer and her team of volunteer forensic photographers, geneticist, and pathologists who work against the clock to put a name to the corpse.
In 2006 the Medicolegal pathology function was transferred from the SAPS to the Health department, meaning Dr.Hans Meyer and her team have to struggle for limited resources and in most cases, they only get the little that is left in the piggy bank- we will look at the issues faced by these group of pathology workers.

As much as this is a morbid topic, the story will deviate from that and will include quirky characters who have a lot of weird and bizarre stories to share.

Press Release:


Speaking to the Dead
They’ve seen it all: gun shots, stab injuries, motor vehicle trauma, and bodies too decomposed to identify. It’s a thankless job – processing and cleaning the deceased. But in the never-ending cycle of violence in South Africa, it’s the men and women working in state morgues, who provide police with the first clues that help solve heinous crimes and get many victims back to their families for burial.


Script:


Speaking to the dead

Opening sequence: Trolleys being pushed-visuals of staff working – sound in the background –

Music ( secret schemer) maybe clean living
V/O it’s Monday morning, barely light – but death knows no business hours. Here at one of the country’s busiest mortuaries, the weekend’s bodies are already streaming in.

[Breathing room]

Claire vlog Link: I'm going to spend the next couple of days at the Johannesburg mortuary to find out more about the people that work here, //so I’m going to take you in with me// –keep an open mind //because honestly when you think about if you live in the greater Gauteng area chances are you're going to end up here and you're going to meet the people I’m about to meet but you won’t be alive for the meeting
V/O Processing thousands of bodies a year, the staff here works around the clock with limited resources to determine cause of death and identify unclaimed bodies.

Up sound Dr Nel [02:40] It gets very busy. We do in excess of 3000 post-mortem examinations in a year, so you can imagine that’s quite a lot of bodies that come through here.

V/O Head pathologist at the Johannesburg mortuary Dr.Nel has conducted hundreds of autopsies. Experience has made her pragmatic about the reality of death, but the violence still strikes home.



Up sound : A lot of it is interpersonal violence true, but it’s not necessarily murder or homicide that kind of issue, but people are who they are and I do believe that we are quite a violent society, unfortunately, and that is what we see the evidence of


V/O The mortuary specifically deals with accidents, suicide, homicide and cases of sudden or unexplained deaths.

Up sound Claire: Do you see a lot of trauma?
Trauma Dr Nel?: Yes that’s what we see because we deal with unnatural deaths and its mostly trauma.

-Breathing space- [ add ambient sound?]

V/O We visited the mortuary after payday weekend -It’s the busiest day of the month and Dr Nel will be performing four autopsies. She has to go through each case file thoroughly for any clue that might help her in determining the cause of death.

[01:21] Claire: So in this process once somebody has been declared dead, you first interact with that through the case files,

Upsound [01:30] Dr Nel Unless you went to the scene but otherwise yes. Most commonly we firstly interact with the documentation.

V/O Autopsies are tightly controlled and access to them is strictly limited to protect the privacy and dignity of the deceased. I am privileged enough to join Dr. Nel as she prepares for what will be a frantic start to the day.

-Breathing space-[visuals of workers wheeling the bodies in]

VO Soon enough, the first bodies start rolling in. On the line-up this morning: a suicide case, a gun-shot victim, as well as two cases that have come directly from a local hospital.
[a bit of breathing space] (maybe time shift)
V/O The autopsy room is a hive of activity… There's no time to waste… Dr Nel and her team get to work. Operating with military precision they carefully dissect, examine and weigh each vital organ, leaving no stone unturned in the search for answers

Link Reaction 2– Behind me is the autopsy room where doctor Nel is performing several autopsies, our cameras weren't allowed in because of family wishes, it a surreal experience to see what pathologist go through to gather evidence to find out why these people died.

Upsound Claire :When I was in the room I realised that you’ve got a dedicated team. You guys were working efficiently, communicating well and it felt like a well-oiled machine.

Upsound DrNel[06:52] There’s a lot of support staff When we go in to do the post-mortem I have a dry assistant - that’s the lady that does the scribing. While I talk, she (or him) writes down exactly what I’m saying. They also receive the specimens from me, like you would have seen - the blood - and seal and then eventually are sent off to the laboratories. And then we have the wet assistants, the people that physically do the - the helps us with the post-mortem examinations.
V/O But despite the staff’s best efforts… this is a system battling under the sheer weight of numbers. Gauteng alone sees over 15000 unnatural deaths annually.

,Upsound Dr Nel :We are sometimes quite short staffed - you can imagine, this is not the kind of speciality most doctors decide to go into ,We work with the police quite often and they also have limited resources


[Breathing space, perhaps?]

Claire link : Thousands of deceased end up here at the Joburg mortuary in Hillbrow, most of them get identified by their loved ones but what happens to those who are not identified.

00:10:31:25 - 00:10:54:19
Upsound Dr Hansmeyer :We have a large portion of our population that remains unidentified and it got us thinking that somebody everybody the Constitution says the Bill of Rights is you have a right to a nationality and a name and an identity

V/O: After seeing the vast number of unclaimed bodies languishing in cold rooms for weeks on end, Forensic Specialist Dr. Hansmeyer was inspired to set up a first-of-its-kind identification Unit at the Johannesburg mortuary

00:12:44:16 - 00:13:20:22
Upsound We wanted to try and ascertain whether or not the unknown the unidentified population in our facilities that died from unnatural causes were foreign or South African
00:20:35:22 - 00:21:15:19
Upsound So after seven days we have a system whereby we can look at our registers and and we can pinpoint those individuals who after seven days have not been identified and then we automatically admit those individuals into Identification Unit

Link Claire: The Role of the unit is to identify unclaimed bodies that come to the mortuary, the body goes through a lodox scan that is a full body scan that checks for bullets, broken bones and other wounds, the body is then brought here for an identification session.

V/O Fingerprints are taken and run through the South African Police Service and Home Affairs data base for comparison. This information is critical in piecing together the puzzle and finding traits that are unique to each individual.

Upsound Craig: we describe every scar every,every tattoo,every marking.We take detailed description and we take photographs as well using the labels.

V/O The unit takes a multidisciplinary approach and is made up Forensic anthropologist, specialist forensic photographers and geneticists. Unit head Craig Keyes and his team bring the full force of modern forensic science to bear on putting names to these unidentified bodies.

Upsound Craig 04:41Bodies that haven’t been identified after seven days come onto our LIST AND ARE THEN PART OF OUR id UNIT WE WILL COLLECT A LOT OF DATA TO TRY TO IDENTIFY THEM , WE WILL TAKE DNA SAMPLES WE WILL TAKE BLOOD, WE TAKE THOROUGH DETAILS OF SCARS AND TATOOS AND IDENTIFYING FEATURES ANYTHING A FAMILY MEMBER MY SAY THIS PARTICULAR PERSON HAD A SCAR


Upsound Craig 06:00This isn’t something that is implemented in other mortuaries as yet,its because of the problem we have here in Joburg because we have so many migrants

V/O Today the team has a particularly gruesome case of an adult male who was hit by a train, as well an elderly male who was found dead near an open grassland.

V/O The Unit works efficiently and diligently and every case is treated with dignity.


Upsound Craig: don’t touch there, touch the side


UpsoundClaire: Are there any particular cases that comes to mind that greately affected you ?
Upsound Craig: One case that comes to my mind is this particular individual that had been abused over many years, I can’t think of any bone that hadn’t been broken multiple times.that affected me particularly…this individual had been beaten for a very long time and ultimately led to her death

V/O Some bodies come in severely decomposed, which makes the process of Identification all the more difficult. It's up to Forensic Anthropologist Allison Gilbert to salvage any clues.

Upsound Allison I head up the Anthropological cases, that is where there is advanced decomposition and there is very little flesh left

Upsound Allison Sometimes it's just bones that have been found in the veld and all you have a bag of bones Its always sadder when they are younger

V/O Because of the complex nature of work being done collaborative efforts become a necessity. [maybe shorten and summarise below upsound]

Upsound we work in conjunction with the anatomy department of the medical school of wits and they can do a rough estimate of demographic - general race group, they can do age and those sort of aspects. Then those cases are taken to the Victim Identification Centre with is run by the police force and they will take the DNA sample and do facial reconstruction.


V/O But all the dedication and skill of the identification unit cannot identify everybody and some cases will remain forever unsolved. [ to get visual of filing cabinets closing]

Link Claire: The bodies that are still unidentified and remain unclaimed get a pauper’s burial here at Olifanstvlei cemetery near Eldorado Park in the south of Johannesburg.

[eerie wind noise]
VO: Here in this desolate part of the cemetery, there are no mourners, no names on tombstones. In each grave three bodies stacked one on the other. All that remains to remember them is a number.

[Breathing space]


VO: Back at the mortuary, there’s little time for reflection, as the workers wash down traces from this morning, one case is replaced by the next and the daily cycle rolls on.
